newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba - DMK investment strong despite EMU uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Buba - DMK investment strong despite EMU uncertainty.

text.p: The German Bundesbank said on Wednesday it saw no indication that investors were responding to uncertainty over Europe's planned monetary union by pulling out of mark investments.
In its April monthly report, the Bundesbank said that foreign financial investment in marks had more than doubled to 1.416 trillion marks in June 1996 from 673 billion at the end of 1990.
"Overall, the mark succeeded in strengthening its position as the second most important investment and reserve currency," the central bank said.

The importance of the mark in this respect added an extra dimension to the switch to a single European currency, meaning that it would be particularly important to ensure a smooth transition and the immediate credibility of the new currency.

"That entails above all a strict interpretation of the convergence criteria in the Maastricht treaty, without any compromises in terms of stability policy, which will leave no room for doubt in the stability policy course of European monetary policy," the Bundesbank said.
At the end of 1996, the mark made up 14.1 percent of world currency reserves, with the dollar taking the lion's share of 62.7 percent and the yen just seven percent.
Mark-denominated eurobonds took third place with 11.2 percent of the total, compared to 37.1 percent in dollars and 17 percent in yen.

International bank deposits in industrial countries were denominated mostly in dollars, at 44.4 percent of the total. The mark made up 15.4 percent and the yen 7.6 percent. The figures exclude foreign direct investment in Germany.
The Bundesbank said in its report that German unification, which had prompted sharply higher public borrowing, had played a large part in the overall increase in investment in mark assets.

Public authorities owed 573 billion marks to foreign investors in June 1996 compared to 219 billion at end-1990, the central bank said. This meant that around 28 percent of total public debt was held abroad.
